subject: Neurology
subtopic: Cranial nerve lesions and facial nerve palsy
vignette: A 58-year-old man reports difficulty chewing. On examination the mandible deviates to the right when he opens his mouth, and the right masseter and temporalis muscles contract weakly against resistance. Facial sensation is intact and there is no facial droop.
question: Which of the following best explains the direction of mandibular deviation in this patient?

options.text: Left CN V motor lesion with an unopposed right pterygoid muscle
Right CN V motor lesion with an unopposed left pterygoid muscle
Right CN VII lesion with unopposed left facial expression muscles
Left CN XII lesion with an unopposed right genioglossus muscle
Right CN X lesion with an unopposed left palatal muscle

explanation_correct: The motor root of CN V innervates the muscles of mastication, including the pterygoids. A right CN V motor lesion weakens the right pterygoid, leaving the contralateral (left) pterygoid unopposed. Unilateral pterygoid contraction pushes the mandible toward the side of the intact muscle, so the jaw deviates to the right, toward the side of the lesion. Sensation is preserved because the lesion involves the motor root.

explanation_incorrect.A: A left CN V motor lesion would leave the right pterygoid unopposed and the jaw would deviate to the left, the opposite direction from these findings.
explanation_incorrect.C: CN VII innervates the muscles of facial expression and does not supply the muscles of mastication; a facial nerve lesion would not deviate the mandible.
explanation_incorrect.D: CN XII is a pure motor nerve to the tongue; a hypoglossal lesion deviates the tongue toward the lesion but does not move the mandible.
explanation_incorrect.E: CN X innervates palatal and laryngeal muscles; a vagal lesion deviates the uvula away from the side of the lesion, not the jaw.

educationalObjective: A CN V motor lesion makes the jaw deviate toward the side of the lesion because the opposite pterygoid acts unopposed.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Cranial nerve lesions and facial nerve palsy
vignette: A 65-year-old woman has difficulty swallowing and a nasal quality to her voice after a brainstem stroke. On examination the left side of the soft palate droops, and the uvula points toward the right side of the mouth.
question: Which of the following lesions best accounts for these findings?

options.text: Right CN X lesion with a weak right soft palate
Left CN IX lesion with a weak left soft palate
Right CN VII lesion with a weak right soft palate
Left CN X lesion with a weak left soft palate
Left CN XII lesion with a weak left soft palate

explanation_correct: CN X (vagus) supplies most of the muscles of the soft palate. With a left vagal lesion the left palatal muscles are weak and the left side collapses, so the intact right side pulls the uvula away from the lesioned side, toward the right. This produces nasal speech and dysphagia alongside the palatal droop.

explanation_incorrect.A: A right CN X lesion would cause a right palatal droop with the uvula deviating to the left, the mirror image of these findings.
explanation_incorrect.B: CN IX innervates stylopharyngeus and supplies oropharyngeal sensation; it does not innervate the palate or produce uvular deviation.
explanation_incorrect.C: CN VII innervates muscles of facial expression and the stapedius, not the soft palate, so it cannot cause a palatal droop or uvular deviation.
explanation_incorrect.E: CN XII innervates the tongue; a left lesion makes the tongue deviate to the left but does not affect the palate or uvula.

educationalObjective: A vagal (CN X) lesion causes the uvula to deviate away from the side of the lesion as the weak side collapses.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Cranial nerve lesions and facial nerve palsy
vignette: A 40-year-old man has difficulty turning his head toward the left when asked to look over his left shoulder. He also has a drooping right shoulder and cannot elevate or shrug that shoulder against resistance. Facial strength, sensation, and tongue protrusion are normal.
question: Which of the following is the most likely lesion?

options.text: Right CN XI lesion affecting the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
Left CN XI lesion affecting the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
Right CN V motor lesion affecting the muscles of mastication
Left CN VII lesion affecting the muscles of facial expression
Right CN XII lesion affecting the intrinsic tongue muscles

explanation_correct: CN XI (spinal accessory) innervates the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. The sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the opposite side, so the right sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the left; a right CN XI lesion weakens the leftward head turn (turning away from the lesion). The trapezius elevates the scapula on its own side, so the right trapezius is weak and the right shoulder droops.

explanation_incorrect.B: A left CN XI lesion would weaken the left sternocleidomastoid (turning the head to the right) and cause a left shoulder droop, the reverse of these findings.
explanation_incorrect.C: CN V motor fibers supply the muscles of mastication; they neither turn the head nor elevate the scapula.
explanation_incorrect.D: CN VII supplies the muscles of facial expression and would produce facial weakness, not a weak head turn or shoulder droop.
explanation_incorrect.E: CN XII supplies the tongue; tongue deviation would occur, not weakness of head turning or shoulder elevation.

educationalObjective: A CN XI lesion weakens head turning away from the side of the lesion and causes an ipsilateral shoulder droop.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Cranial nerve lesions and facial nerve palsy
vignette: A 70-year-old man has slurred speech and difficulty manipulating food in his mouth. When he protrudes his tongue it points toward the left, and the left side of the tongue appears wasted with fasciculations.
question: Which of the following is the most likely lesion?

options.text: Right CN X lesion
Left CN VII lesion
Right CN XI lesion
Right CN V motor lesion
Left CN XII lower motor neuron lesion

explanation_correct: CN XII (hypoglossal) is a pure motor nerve to the tongue. A lower motor neuron lesion of the left hypoglossal nerve weakens the left tongue muscles, so the intact right genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak side and the tongue deviates to the left, toward the lesion. This is remembered as licking wounds on the side of the lesion; ipsilateral wasting and fasciculations confirm an LMN lesion.

explanation_incorrect.A: CN X innervates the palate and larynx; a lesion would alter the voice and deviate the uvula, not deviate the tongue.
explanation_incorrect.B: CN VII innervates the muscles of facial expression; it does not supply the tongue musculature.
explanation_incorrect.C: CN XI supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; tongue deviation is not a feature of an accessory nerve lesion.
explanation_incorrect.D: CN V motor fibers supply the muscles of mastication, which would deviate the jaw toward the lesion rather than the tongue.

educationalObjective: A hypoglossal (CN XII) lower motor neuron lesion makes the tongue deviate toward the side of the lesion on protrusion.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Cranial nerve lesions and facial nerve palsy
vignette: A 34-year-old woman wakes up with right-sided facial weakness. She cannot fully close her right eye and has lost taste sensation over the anterior two-thirds of her tongue. The forehead is involved, and there is no limb weakness or sensory loss elsewhere.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and underlying cause?

options.text: Ischemic stroke due to middle cerebral artery occlusion
Ramsay Hunt syndrome due to varicella zoster reactivation
Bell palsy due to herpes simplex virus reactivation
Lyme disease due to Borrelia burgdorferi infection
Sarcoidosis due to noncaseating granuloma formation

explanation_correct: Bell palsy is the most common cause of peripheral (lower motor neuron) facial palsy and usually develops after herpes simplex virus reactivation. The entire ipsilateral face, including the forehead, is weak because the facial nucleus or nerve is involved. Treatment is glucocorticoids with or without acyclovir, and aberrant regeneration can occur during recovery.

explanation_incorrect.A: An MCA stroke produces an upper motor neuron lesion with contralateral lower-face weakness that spares the forehead and is accompanied by limb findings.
explanation_incorrect.B: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is varicella zoster reactivation with ipsilateral facial paralysis, otalgia, and vesicles near the auditory canal, none of which are described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Lyme disease can cause a peripheral facial palsy but is not the most common cause and would usually include a tick exposure or erythema migrans.
explanation_incorrect.E: Sarcoidosis may cause facial nerve palsy from granulomas but is uncommon and typically accompanied by other systemic findings.

educationalObjective: Bell palsy from HSV reactivation is the most common peripheral facial palsy and is treated with steroids with or without acyclovir.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Cranial nerve lesions and facial nerve palsy
vignette: A 60-year-old man has right-sided facial weakness that spares the forehead. He can wrinkle his brow and close both eyes normally, but the right lower face droops when he smiles. He has no hearing loss, altered taste, or eye dryness.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this lesion?

options.text: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron lesion of CN VII in the facial canal
Contralateral upper motor neuron lesion with forehead sparing from bilateral cortical innervation
Ipsilateral lesion of the facial nucleus in the pons
Bilateral lower motor neuron lesions of both facial nerves
Contralateral lesion of the hypoglossal nerve

explanation_correct: An upper motor neuron lesion in the motor cortex or corticobulbar tract produces contralateral weakness of the lower muscles of facial expression. The forehead is spared because the upper face receives bilateral cortical innervation, so one hemispheric lesion leaves it functional. This contrasts with a lower motor neuron lesion, which affects the entire ipsilateral face including the forehead.

explanation_incorrect.A: An ipsilateral lower motor neuron lesion of CN VII would involve both the upper and lower face on that side, so the forehead would not be spared.
explanation_incorrect.C: A lesion of the facial nucleus in the pons is a lower motor neuron lesion and would weaken the whole ipsilateral face, including the forehead.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bilateral lower motor neuron lesions would cause bilateral facial weakness including both foreheads, not an isolated right lower-face droop.
explanation_incorrect.E: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue, not the muscles of facial expression, and would not cause a facial droop.

educationalObjective: Central facial lesions affect the contralateral lower face only because the upper face has bilateral cortical innervation.
